value: ClinicMind is an all-in-one healthcare SaaS platform helping practices improve retention, reduce provider burnout, and manage revenue across the care lifecycle. As the company began investing in UX maturity, I joined as the second designer to lead redesign across five core products, for clinical and administrative users alike.

With a 20-year legacy, every product decision had been made by engineers. Design was a newborn function. On day one I faced not a design problem but a trust deficit: no authority, no collaboration process, no language to prove design was useful.
Opening Figma and restyling buttons would only brand me "the person who makes things pretty."

blocks.label: The real first problem
blocks.value: Before pushing any design, I had to earn the right to be heard.

blocks.label: ClinicMind's platform — a 20-year, all-in-one healthcare SaaS

indexedSections.title: Four moves to earn the room

blocks.title: Make the team see a problem they'd stopped noticing

value: The first hard battle: engineers couldn't feel the problem. The system was complex and the flows convoluted — but after 20 years, that was just "how it is." You can't push a problem nobody can see.

So I didn't argue about design. I ran discovery calls with our core users — physicians — whose time is scarce and hard to get. One fact landed: our doctors spend a huge share of the day not on patient care, but on note-taking, scheduling, and fighting with insurers.
I brought that back untouched. I didn't say "your design is bad." I said:

blocks.value: Our physicians spend half their day away from patients.
blocks.attribution: How I reframed the problem to the team

blocks.value: That turned an abstract "UX issue" into a human and business problem the team couldn't ignore — and engineering saw it. That's the translation work: turning the doctor's language into language engineers act on.

blocks.label: Discovery calls with physicians — synthesis boards from the care-plan and daily-task sessions

blocks.title: Sell "slow down to speed up" to a team hungry to ship

value: Next, a harder sell: stop piling on features and build a design system first.

Deeply counter-intuitive at the time: the team wanted output, and I was asking for a foundation with no short-term deliverable — in a regulated clinical domain whose vocabulary I was still learning. My argument wasn't "it'll look better." It was ROI math: with two designers against 7+ engineers, negotiating every page from scratch means we never catch up. With an Atomic Design component library and clear documentation, every feature becomes assembly.

blocks.label: The argument that landed
blocks.value: Slow down once, so everyone moves faster after. Framed as ROI, not taste, the product owner bought in.

blocks.label: Atomic Design — the methodology behind the Vericle Design System

blocks.value: The system itself: color, typography, effects and radii, spacing, and the component library — each specified on real EHR surfaces rather than in the abstract, so engineering had something concrete to build against.

value: What actually accelerated collaboration was changing how the team communicated. With no prototypes or specs, everything lived in words — everyone pictured something different, and reviews spun. So I did two high-leverage things:

items.label: Artifacts over words
items.title: Prototypes replace description
items.desc: One shared artifact per review, instead of five imagined versions.

items.label: Produce once, reuse endlessly
items.title: 30+ recorded demos
items.desc: Every page and interaction on video with Figma specs, open to dev and business.

blocks.value: With the product owners, we aimed that effort at the highest-impact parts of the system — Care Plans and Daily Task Management — where sketches and prototypes let us gather feedback and iterate fast.

blocks.label: Interactive prototypes — the thing everyone points at

blocks.value: The demos let stakeholders see features early, turning them from recipients of a surprise change into co-builders. Alignment shifted from repeated debate to one visible truth.

blocks.label: The demo library — 30+ recorded walkthroughs, always available to the dev and business teams

blocks.title: The finish line is a 1:1 build, not an approved mock

value: "Driving design" never meant "the mock got approved." It meant "the design shipped as intended."

Previously engineers implemented from their own interpretation, and the result drifted. Now, with the design system as a shared language and 30+ demos plus Figma specs as handoff, engineering could match my intent down to the interactions.

blocks.label: What actually changed
blocks.value: Communication stopped being a one-off handoff and became a continuously closing loop.

indexedSections.title: Design, embedded in the team's daily work

items.title: A design system from scratch
items.desc: Atomic Design, clearly documented — the team's shared language.

items.title: 30+ demos as shared memory
items.desc: The team's source of truth for every flow and interaction.

items.title: Cleaner core interfaces
items.desc: Surfaces like the appointment dashboard got cleaner and better organized.

items.title: Reliable, high-quality shipping
items.desc: High-fidelity builds landed consistently on minimal design resources.

blocks.value: With the style guide and design system in place, the appointment dashboard is noticeably cleaner and more organized.

blocks.label: The redesigned appointment dashboard — cleaner and more organized

blocks.value: The real result wasn't how well I designed — it was making communication a team capability.

indexedSections.title: Let everyone see the same truth

value: In a place with no design culture, a designer's biggest output isn't mockups — it's getting the team thinking in terms of design. Not through authority, but by letting everyone see the same truth.

blocks.label: What I take with me
blocks.value: Advocating for design quality starts before you have any formal power — and building that influence from the ground up is where I'm at my best.
